lessons.title: Close-up: a horse and a watcher

zoom.label: A white horse in a jewelled harness, at the bottom left

c1.text: Level one: the king orders his women and pages killed. Now zoom into the bottom left: a white horse in a jewelled harness, pulled by its reins.

zoom.label: A white horse in a jewelled harness, at the bottom left

c1q.text: Why is a horse here, among the women and the gold?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record RF 2346, 'Mort de Sardanapale' (the Salon booklet's text, quoted in the record; our translations)
Philadelphia Museum of Art, 'The Death of Sardanapalus', 1844, Eugène Delacroix (label text of its replica)
A. Jal, Esquisses, croquis, pochades ... sur le Salon de 1827 (Paris, 1828), p. 313 (our translations)

c1m.text: Nothing that pleased the king may outlive him: not his women, not even his horses.

c1a.text: The rebels are outside; this is the king's own household.

correction.tempting: The booklet says rebels besiege the palace, and smoke rises beyond the room.
correction.truth: The booklet says the king orders even his favourite horses killed: nothing that served his pleasures may survive him.
correction.evidence: Salon booklet text, quoted in the Louvre record. Philadelphia Museum of Art: he orders even his horses and dogs destroyed.

c1b.text: Yes. The booklet says he orders even his favourite horses and dogs killed, so that nothing that served his pleasures outlives him.

c1c.text: He's pulling it, but not to safety.

correction.tempting: The man pulls it forward by its reins, away from the bed.
correction.truth: The booklet's king orders even his favourite horses killed, so that nothing that served his pleasures survives him.
correction.evidence: Salon booklet text, quoted in the Louvre record. Philadelphia Museum of Art: he orders even his horses and dogs destroyed.

zoom.label: The bearded man in a turban at the top left, on the bed

c2.text: Level one: from his bed, the king gives the orders. Now zoom into the top left, at the head of the bed: the king himself.

zoom.label: The bearded man in a turban at the top left, on the bed

c2q.text: What is the king doing while his orders are carried out?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record RF 2346, 'Mort de Sardanapale' (the Salon booklet's text, quoted in the record; our translations)
A. Jal, Esquisses, croquis, pochades ... sur le Salon de 1827 (Paris, 1828), p. 313 (our translations)
Philadelphia Museum of Art, 'The Death of Sardanapalus', 1844, Eugène Delacroix (label text of its replica)

c2m.text: Others do the killing; the king, on his pyre, only lies back and watches.

c2a.text: He gave the orders, but he isn't shouting now.

correction.tempting: The booklet says he orders his household killed.
correction.truth: He lies back, head propped on his hand, and watches. Jal wrote that his eyes 'feast' on the scene (our translation).
correction.evidence: Salon booklet, in the Louvre record: lying on a superb bed. Jal (1828). Philadelphia Museum of Art: destroyed 'in his presence'.

c2b.text: Yes. He lies back, head propped on his hand. The critic Jal wrote that his eyes 'feast' on the cruel pleasures before closing for ever (our translation).

c2c.text: The pyre is there, but he isn't lighting it.

correction.tempting: The booklet puts his bed on top of an immense pyre.
correction.truth: He lies still, head on his hand, watching the killing done 'in his presence', as Philadelphia's museum puts it.
correction.evidence: Philadelphia Museum of Art. Jal (1828): his eyes 'feast' on the scene (our translation). The pose is plain in the crop.

extends.concept: From the women and pages the level names to the horses: why a horse stands among the killing

c1q.what_you_learn: The horse is there because the booklet's king orders even his favourite horses and dogs killed, so that nothing that served his pleasures survives him.

regionSources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record RF 2346, 'Mort de Sardanapale' (description field: extract of the second supplement to the Salon booklet of 1827-1828; our translations)
regionSources.quote: Sardanapale donne l'ordre à ses eunuques et aux officiers du palais, d'égorger ses femmes, ses pages, jusqu'à ses chevaux et ses chiens favoris ; aucun des objets qui avaient servi à ses plaisirs ne devait lui survivre
regionSources.supports: Our translation: Sardanapalus orders his eunuchs and palace officers to cut the throats of his women, his pages, even his favourite horses and dogs; none of the objects that had served his pleasures was to survive him. Gives the reason a horse is in the scene.

c1q.confidence: High for the reason (the booklet's text via the Louvre record and the Philadelphia Museum of Art's label agree). The region: the white horse is the only horse in the picture, so the booklet's horses and Jal's horse's head can only be this one; no source gives its position in words, which is plain in the photo.
c1q.notes: Ledger claims sardan-006 (booklet subject: Louvre record + PMA), sardan-029 (Jal's horse's head), sardan-005 (our looking: a servant drags a white horse in jewelled harness at lower left). The level's n1b deliberately names only the women and pages, so the horses are new here. 'Rebels' and 'safety' are real readings of what is in the crop (the siege, the man pulling the reins), not sourced claims about this horse; their cards state only sourced facts. Not used: the man's identity (eunuch, officer or slave), which no source gives.

extends.concept: From the king who gives the orders (level) to what he does while they are carried out

c2q.what_you_learn: The king does no killing and lights nothing: he lies back on his bed, head on his hand, and watches, the destruction done in his presence.

c2c.quote: La destruction de tant d'êtres vivans sur le bûcher du tyran
c2c.supports: Our translation: the destruction of so many living beings on the tyrant's pyre. The pyre is there (also in the booklet), but the king's eyes 'feast': he watches.
c2c.readVia: Saved Internet Archive OCR text in the research folder, 16 Oct 2026

c2q.confidence: High: the booklet (lying on his bed), Jal (his eyes feast on the scene) and the Philadelphia label (in his presence) agree, and the pose is plain in the crop. That this bearded, turbaned man is the king is our identification from the booklet (the man lying on the bed) and Jal ('the pose of Sardanapalus'); no source names his position in words.
c2q.notes: Ledger claims sardan-006 (booklet + PMA), sardan-029 (Jal), sardan-004 (our looking: the bearded, turbaned king at upper left, head propped on his hand). Who finally lights the pyre in the booklet (Baleah, sardan-007) is Louvre-only and NOT said; the c2c card says only that he lies still and watches. The level never describes his pose, so the close-up is new.
